0.title: Malachi: The Sun of Righteousness
0.overview:
Malachi is the last of the twelve Minor Prophets and the last book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles (the Hebrew Bible places the Writings after the Prophets and ends with Chronicles). It is a conversation with a bored congregation: the temple rebuilt, the services on time, and the whole thing gone flat. Serving God is a weariness (1:13), and they cannot see what they get out of it (3:14).

We know nothing about the prophet except his name, which the ESV notes means "my messenger" — fitting for a book that ends by promising the greatest of the messengers. He wrote after the temple was finished, probably in the mid-400s BC, the days of Ezra and Nehemiah, when their problems were current: careless priests, mixed marriages, neglected tithes.

The book is built as six disputes. God makes a statement, the people answer back with But you say, and God takes their objections seriously enough to answer every one.

God's love (1:2-5). "How have you loved us?" He points to his choice of Jacob. God's honour (1:6-2:9). The priests bring blind and lame animals they would never offer the governor. Faithlessness (2:10-16). Men are discarding the wives of their youth, and God was the witness at those weddings. Justice (2:17-3:5). "Where is the God of justice?" — he is coming, and the question will be who can endure it. Robbery (3:6-12). Withheld tithes. Profit (3:13-4:3). "It is vain to serve God", and the promised day of difference.

Two things in this book are easy to misuse. The tithing promise of 3:10 is God's word to a farming nation under the covenant of Moses about rain and harvests, not a guarantee that individual givers will get rich; it teaches that God notices what we do with money and is extravagantly generous, and no believer is less precious to him for having little to give. The New Testament keeps the generosity and changes its spring: God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7). And the passage on divorce (2:13-16) condemns treachery against a faithful wife; it is not a club to beat those whose marriages have already broken, for whom this book's first words and last promise are the answer.

Malachi points to Christ repeatedly. The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (3:1), preceded by the messenger Mark sees in John the Baptist (Mark 1:2). He comes like a refiner's fire to purify (3:2-3). And for those who fear God's name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (4:2), which is what Zechariah sang over the cradle of his son: the sunrise shall visit us from on high (Luke 1:78).

The tenderest moment is easy to miss: while everyone else complained, those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and God wrote their conversations in a book of remembrance (3:16). They will be his treasured possession (3:17).

Our Old Testament ends with a warning hanging in the air and four centuries without a new prophet's book, until a man in camel's hair appeared and behind him came the Lord to his temple. The last word of our English Old Testament is "destruction"; the answer to it is a cross, where Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). Malachi's people asked how God had loved them. That is the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — How Have You Loved Us?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: "I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" (vv. 1-2). God's answer is his choice: Is not Esau Jacob's brother? ... Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated (vv. 2-3). Edom may rebuild, but God will tear down (v. 4), and Israel will say, Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love for his people rests on his own choice, not on anything in them, and it is visible in their history.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi. "I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" "Is not Esau Jacob's brother?" declares the LORD. "Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated. I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals of the desert." If Edom says, "We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins," the LORD of hosts says, "They may build, but I will tear down, and they will be called 'the wicked country,' and 'the people with whom the LORD is angry forever.'" Your own eyes shall see this, and you shall say, "Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last of the twelve Minor Prophets, and in Christian Bibles the last book of the Old Testament. The temple has been rebuilt for some decades, the excitement of the return has worn off, and Israel has settled into a dull, disappointed religion. Nobody worships idols on the rooftops any more; they are simply bored with God.

The prophet's name is given (the ESV notes that Malachi means "my messenger"), which fits a book that talks about messengers all the way through, and ends by promising the greatest of them.

Six times God makes a statement, the people answer back, and God replies: But you say is the drumbeat of Malachi, an argument with a congregation that thinks it has a case.

God's opening statement is not a rebuke. It is four words: I have loved you. Everything else in the book stands on that.

And the answer comes back: How have you loved us? Look at the life we are living: a small province, a modest temple, poor harvests, foreign governors. Where is this love?

It is the question of every disappointed believer: not "is there a God?" but "does he love me, given all this?"

God's answer is to take them back before either nation existed, to two brothers in one womb. Is not Esau Jacob's brother? Esau was the elder, with every natural right, and God chose Jacob, the younger, the schemer.

This hard language must be handled carefully. Paul quotes it: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (Rom 9:13), and uses it to teach that God's choice does not depend on human merit.

In the Bible the pair "love" and "hate" is often the language of choosing and passing over. Jesus used the same pattern when he said that anyone coming to him must hate his own father and mother (Luke 14:26), meaning that every other loyalty must come second; Matthew gives the same saying as loving them more than him (Matt 10:37). God is not describing a spite against Esau the man but the fact that he chose Jacob's line to carry his promise, and did not choose Edom's.

And this is God's evidence for his love. Why are you here at all, complaining about your harvest? Because I chose your father Jacob when there was no reason to.

Christians should hear this personally. If you are in Christ, the answer to "how have you loved me?" is not your circumstances but your election: God chose you in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4), and Christ died for you when you were an enemy (Rom 5:10).

Edom's determination to rebuild is exactly what Obadiah had confronted, and the verdict is the same. Human resolve cannot outlast God's decision.

And the conclusion Israel is meant to draw is not smugness but worship, and it reaches past their own borders: Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel! God's greatness is not a local matter, which is the theme of verse 11.

Is this the election of nations or individuals? Malachi speaks of the nations Israel and Edom, as verse 4 shows. Paul quotes it of the two individuals, chosen before birth not because of works but because of him who calls (Rom 9:11–13). Both are true: the nations came from the two men, and God’s choice of Jacob was his free grace. “Hated” means not chosen, in Hebrew idiom (cf. Gen 29:30–31). Many Christians, especially in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, read Paul as speaking of God choosing nations for their place in history rather than persons for salvation. This commentary holds, with the Reformed confessions, that Paul means persons: he stresses that the choice came before the twins had done anything (Rom 9:11), and the objection he answers next, Is there injustice on God’s part? (Rom 9:14), would hardly arise otherwise. Those who read it differently are brothers. Nor is the hatred blind spite: verse 4 ties God’s anger to Edom’s wickedness, and the law still told Israel, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).
verseByVerse.note: “Malachi” means “my messenger” (ESV note). He prophesied around 450–430 BC, perhaps in Nehemiah’s time — probably the last of the Old Testament prophets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Polluted Food on My Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? (v. 6). The priests offer polluted food and say the LORD's table may be despised (v. 7): blind, lame and sick animals they would never dare give the governor (vv. 8-9). God would rather the doors were shut than have such worship (v. 10), for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations (v. 11). They find it a weariness (vv. 12-13), and God says, I am a great King (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship that costs nothing and gives God the leftovers insults a great King.

verseByVerse.quote: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the LORD of hosts to you, O priests, who despise my name. But you say, 'How have we despised your name?' By offering polluted food upon my altar. But you say, 'How have we polluted you?' By saying that the LORD's table may be despised. When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? says the LORD of hosts. And now entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With such a gift from your hand, will he show favor to any of you? says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns to the clergy, and the argument is simple. Everyone understands that a son honours his father and a servant respects his master. So: where is my honor?

And the priests are genuinely baffled: How have we despised your name? They have not despised it deliberately. That is the point of this whole book. The sins Malachi exposes are not scandals; they are the slow, unnoticed slide of people who still turn up.

When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? God's law required unblemished animals (Lev 22:20). The priests were accepting blind, lame and sick beasts: the animals a farmer could not sell, brought to God because they were no use for anything else.

Then the decisive question: Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? Try offering the Persian governor a lame sheep as your taxes and see how it goes. They would never insult a human official the way they were insulting God.

We give God the tired end of the day, the money left after everything else, the attention left over once the phone has had its share. Nobody decides to do it; it simply happens. The cure is not guilt but the chapter's first words: leftovers are what we give someone we have stopped believing loves us, and God's I have loved you (v. 2) is what rekindles a whole-hearted gift.

The sarcasm of verse 9 is heavy: go on, ask God to bless you, with that in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you, says the LORD of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering. For my name will be great among the nations, says the LORD of hosts. But you profane it when you say that the Lord's table is polluted, and its fruit, that is, its food, may be despised. But you say, 'What a weariness this is,' and you snort at it, says the LORD of hosts. You bring what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick, and this you bring as your offering! Shall I accept that from your hand? says the LORD. Cursed be the cheat who has a male in his flock, and vows it, and yet sacrifices to the Lord what is blemished. For I am a great King, says the LORD of hosts, and my name will be feared among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is a startling sentence from God. He wishes someone would shut the doors of the temple and stop the services altogether.

Half-hearted worship is worse than none, because it teaches everyone watching that God is not worth much.

Now the horizon opens wide. While the priests in Jerusalem are shuffling sick animals onto the altar, God says that his name will be great among the nations from one end of the earth to the other, with a pure offering in every place. (The ESV notes the verbs may be read as present: "is great".)

To a Jew, for whom worship happened at one altar, offered by one family, this was almost unthinkable. God announces worship in every place, from the nations. Jesus told the woman at the well the same thing: the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John 4:21–23).

There is a sharp rebuke inside the promise. God is saying: if you will not honour me, others will. He is never left without worshippers.

The heart-condition behind everything: What a weariness this is, and they snort at it.

That is an honest description of how a person can feel about church and prayer, and the honesty is a mercy. God knows when we are bored with him, and it is better to admit it than to perform.

What they brought included animals taken by violence: stolen goods offered to God. It is possible to be generous to God with what was never rightly ours.

The final case is the worst: a man who has a good animal, promises it to God, and then swaps it for a damaged one. Not poverty; deceit.

And the reason this matters is given in five words: I am a great King. The question is never what we can spare but who he is.

And this chapter, which begins with God saying I have loved you, drives us to the one offering that was never blemished. Christ was a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:19), and he was not the leftover of the flock but the beloved Son.

Is the “pure offering” the Mass? Malachi foresees the nations worshipping God everywhere, in the language of his own day. The New Testament names the offerings of the new age: praise and good works (Heb 13:15–16), our bodies (Rom 12:1), and the Gentiles themselves (Rom 15:16). Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all and is never repeated (Heb 10:10–14).

1.title: I Have Loved You
1.overview:
God opens with "I have loved you", and when the people ask how, he points to his free choice of Jacob over Esau (vv. 1-5).

Then he confronts the priests who offer blind, lame and sick animals they would never give their governor; he would rather the temple doors were shut, for his name will be great among the nations, and he is a great King (vv. 6-14).
1.theology:
God's love for his people rests on his own choice rather than on anything in them (vv. 2-3; Rom 9:13).

The evidence of God's love is not our circumstances but his electing grace (v. 2).

Human determination cannot outlast God's decision (v. 4).

Worship that gives God what we would not dare give an earthly official despises his name (vv. 6-8).

Half-hearted worship is worse than none, because it teaches onlookers that God is not worth much (v. 10).

God will be worshipped by the nations in every place, whether or not his own people honour him (v. 11).

Weariness with God is a real spiritual condition, and God sees it behind the routine (v. 13).

The measure of our giving is not what we can spare but who God is: a great King (v. 14).
1.examples:
A congregation that argues back, six times over.

Two brothers in one womb, and a choice made before either had done anything.

A lame sheep offered to God and never to the tax office.

God wishing someone would lock the church doors.

Incense offered to God in every place on earth, while the temple sulks.

Worshippers snorting at the service.

A man who vows the good animal and swaps in the damaged one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God warns the priests: if they will not give honor to my name, he will curse their blessings (vv. 1-3). His covenant with Levi was one of life and peace, and the model priest walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity (vv. 4-6). For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge ... for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts (v. 7). But these priests have caused many to stumble and shown partiality, so God has made them despised and abased (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who teach God's word are messengers, and when they corrupt it they bring down the people with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O priests, this command is for you. If you will not listen, if you will not take it to heart to give honor to my name, says the LORD of hosts, then I will send the curse upon you and I will curse your blessings. Indeed, I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart. Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and spread dung on your faces, the dung of your offerings, and you shall be taken away with it. So shall you know that I have sent this command to you, that my covenant with Levi may stand, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warning is addressed to the clergy, and the phrase that recurs is take it to heart. Twice God says they will not do it. The problem is not ignorance but inattention; they have heard it all and it has not landed anywhere.

I will curse your blessings is a chilling phrase. The priests' job was to pronounce blessing over the people. God says the blessings themselves will turn.

The language is deliberately disgusting. (The ESV notes offspring is literally "seed".) When an animal was sacrificed, the waste was carried outside the camp and burned. God says he will take that refuse and smear it on the faces of the priests who offered it, and they will be carried out with it.

What they treated as acceptable worship is, to God, the rubbish from the back of the altar.

And the aim of even this severe word is restoration: that my covenant with Levi may stand. God is not finished with the priesthood. He is clearing away what has spoiled it.

verseByVerse.quote: My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave them to him. It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me. He stood in awe of my name. True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity. For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. But you have turned aside from the way. You have caused many to stumble by your instruction. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the LORD of hosts, and so I make you despised and abased before all the people, inasmuch as you do not keep my ways but show partiality in your instruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now God describes what a priest was meant to be, and it is a beautiful portrait. The covenant God made with Levi brought life and peace, and it produced a man who feared me and stood in awe of my name. Reverence came first; everything else grew from it.

Four marks of a faithful minister follow. True instruction was in his mouth (the ESV notes this may be rendered "law"): what he taught was accurate. No wrong was found on his lips: he did not shade it to please anyone. He walked with me in peace and uprightness: his life matched his teaching. And he turned many from iniquity: real people actually changed.

No priest of Levi's line matched this portrait for long. One has matched it completely: Jesus, the high priest who is holy, innocent, unstained (Heb 7:26), in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet 2:22), and who still turns many from iniquity.

A priest is to guard knowledge, like a man entrusted with something valuable that others need. And he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts, the word that gives this book its name. Malachi is God's messenger; the priests were meant to be too.

The charge is that their teaching has made many stumble, and that they show partiality: one ruling for the influential, another for the poor. Teaching that bends for important people corrupts everything.

And the result is that the priests are despised by the very people they flattered. Honour cannot be bought with compromise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — The Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Have we not all one Father? Why then are they faithless to one another? (v. 10). Judah has married the daughter of a foreign god (vv. 11-12). They flood the altar with tears and wonder why God does not accept them: because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant (vv. 13-14). God made them one and seeks Godly offspring; so guard yourselves in your spirit (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God is a witness at every wedding, and he takes the breaking of that covenant as seriously as any sin in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another, profaning the covenant of our fathers? Judah has been faithless, and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the LORD, which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god. May the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob any descendant of the man who does this, who brings an offering to the LORD of hosts!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Malachi turns from the priests to the whole community, and begins with the ground of all human obligation: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Because one God made us, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him.

The first charge is marriage to the daughter of a foreign god. This is about religion, not race: Israel's law had always welcomed foreigners who came to trust the God of Israel, and Ruth the Moabite is in the Messiah's family tree. The problem is marrying into the worship of another god, which is what Ezra and Nehemiah were dealing with at this time (Ezra 9–10; Neh 13:23–27).

And the sting is in the last phrase: the man brings an offering to the LORD of hosts. He keeps coming to church. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of this line is "any who wakes and answers".)

The New Testament instinct is the same: believers are to marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39). This is not snobbery about other people; it is realism about what marriage does to the deepest loyalties of a life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this second thing you do. You cover the LORD's altar with tears, with weeping and groaning because he no longer regards the offering or accepts it with favor from your hand. But you say, "Why does he not?" Because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant. Did he not make them one, with a portion of the Spirit in their union? And what was the one God seeking? Godly offspring. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth. "For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence, says the LORD of hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second charge is the one this chapter is remembered for. The altar is wet with tears, men weeping and groaning because God will not accept them, and utterly baffled as to why. Emotional worship is not the same as acceptable worship. You can weep at the altar and be in the wrong.

The reason is domestic: what they have done to their wives.

Three phrases repay attention. The wife of your youth: the woman he married when they were both young, now older, and set aside for someone else. Your companion: a partner and friend, not a possession. Your wife by covenant: marriage is a covenant, not an arrangement, and God was the witness at it.

Every wedding has a third party present, whether the couple know it or not.

Did he not make them one, with a portion of the Spirit in their union? The ESV notes several difficulties in the Hebrew of this verse, and gives an alternative rendering. The sense is clear enough: God "made them one", as Genesis says, and he was seeking Godly offspring, children raised in a home where God is honoured.

Then the command, twice: guard yourselves in your spirit (the ESV notes this may read "take care"). Faithfulness is guarded on the inside, long before anything happens on the outside, and not by willpower alone: the God who gave a portion of the Spirit to the union gives his Spirit to his people, with his word, prayer and the help of other believers, to keep that guard.

The ESV notes that this verse is difficult, and gives the older, familiar rendering in its margin: "The LORD, the God of Israel, says that he hates divorce". The Hebrew reads literally "for he hates sending away", and it is unclear whether the one who hates is God or the husband: older versions took it of God (the KJV has "he hateth putting away"), while the ESV takes it of the man who divorces the wife he does not love. Either way the message is the same, and it is severe. The man who discards his wife covers his garment with violence: the treachery shows on him like blood on clothing.

A pastoral word is necessary here. Scripture does not treat all divorce identically; Jesus allowed for it in some circumstances, and Paul in another, and the Bible everywhere protects the wronged party rather than trapping them. What Malachi condemns is treachery: breaking a covenant because you have tired of the person you made it with.

Behind every faithful marriage stands a greater one. Paul calls marriage a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:25, 31–32), and Christ is the husband who never tires of his bride, faithful in every way we have not been, and his faithfulness is counted to us: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

And for readers who carry the pain of a broken marriage, whether they were the betrayer or the betrayed, the whole book is the answer. It begins with I have loved you and ends with healing in the wings of the sun of righteousness. God takes covenant-breaking seriously because he takes people seriously, and he is in the business of forgiving and restoring exactly this.

Is divorce ever allowed, and may a divorced person remarry? God hates the treachery of a man who abandons the wife of his youth (v. 16). Jesus allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matt 19:9), and Paul frees a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor 7:15); the Reformed confessions hold that in those cases the innocent party may remarry (the Westminster Confession 24.5–6). Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: anyone being abused should seek safety at once, and the church's elders should help judge each case and stand with the one wronged. Malachi's own words point the same way: God condemns the man who covers his garment with violence, not the one who flees it. Some faithful Christians hold that remarriage is never allowed while the first spouse lives; this commentary holds the confessional view as the better reading. Divorce on other grounds is sin, but it is not beyond forgiveness in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative rendering of v. 16: the LORD “says that he hates divorce.”

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17 — You Have Wearied the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You have wearied the LORD with your words — by saying that evildoers please him, and by asking, Where is the God of justice? (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Cynicism about God's justice wearies him, and his answer is to announce that he is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: You have wearied the LORD with your words. But you say, "How have we wearied him?" By saying, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delights in them." Or by asking, "Where is the God of justice?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by opening the fourth dispute, and this time the charge is that their talk has wearied God. God is never tired, but he can be worn out by a certain kind of conversation.

What wears him out is cynicism. They had been saying two things. First, that God is indifferent to morality: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD. Look around, they said; the crooked prosper and God seems pleased with them. Second, the weary question: Where is the God of justice?

This is the complaint of people who have watched injustice go unpunished for a long time, and it differs from honest lament. Habakkuk asked how long and waited at his watchpost for an answer. These men have stopped expecting one; they are simply grumbling.

And God's answer is the next verse of the book, which happens to be one of the great promises of the Old Testament: Behold, I send my messenger (3:1). They asked where the God of justice was. He replies that he is coming, and that the real question will be who can endure his arrival.

2.title: The Wife of Your Youth
2.overview:
God warns the careless priests and sets beside them his covenant with Levi, the faithful priest who taught truly and turned many from iniquity (vv. 1-9).

Then he charges the people with marrying into the worship of a foreign god and with faithlessness to the wife of their youth, a covenant at which he was the witness (vv. 10-16). Last, they have wearied him by asking, "Where is the God of justice?" (v. 17).
2.theology:
God's severest words to his ministers aim at restoring, not abolishing, the ministry (v. 4).

A faithful teacher's marks are accurate teaching, integrity, a matching life, and people actually turned from sin (vv. 6-7).

Teaching that shows partiality corrupts the covenant and loses the respect it courted (vv. 8-9).

Because one God created us, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him (v. 10).

Marriage into the worship of another god profanes what God loves; the issue is religious, not racial (v. 11).

Tears at the altar are no substitute for faithfulness at home (v. 13).

Marriage is a covenant at which God himself is the witness, and he seeks godly offspring from it (vv. 14-15; Gen 2:24; Matt 19:6).

Faithfulness is guarded in the spirit, long before anything shows (vv. 15-16).

Cynicism about God's justice wearies him, and his answer is that he is coming (v. 17).
2.examples:
Blessings that turn into curses in the mouths of careless priests.

The refuse from the altar smeared on the faces of those who offered it.

A priest described as a man who guarded knowledge for others.

One ruling for the influential and another for the poor.

An altar wet with tears, and God not listening.

A third party present at every wedding.

Treachery that shows on a man like blood on his coat.

People who ask where the God of justice is and no longer expect an answer.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>"Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>2</sup>But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap.<sup>3</sup>He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years.<sup>5</sup>"Then I will draw near to you for judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against those who swear falsely, against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, against those who thrust aside the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>6</sup>"For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed.<sup>7</sup>From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need.<sup>11</sup>I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your soil, and your vine in the field shall not fail to bear, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>12</sup>Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>13</sup>"Your words have been hard against me, says the LORD. But you say, 'How have we spoken against you?'<sup>14</sup>You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What is the profit of our keeping his charge or of walking as in mourning before the LORD of hosts?<sup>15</sup>And now we call the arrogant blessed. Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape.'"<sup>16</sup>Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lord Will Suddenly Come to His Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (v. 1). But who can endure the day of his coming? He is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap (v. 2), who will purify the sons of Levi so that their offerings please God again (vv. 3-4). Then he will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who cheat workers of wages, and those who wrong the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They asked where the God of justice was; he answers that he is coming, and the question is who can stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD. Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years. "Then I will draw near to you for judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against those who swear falsely, against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, against those who thrust aside the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked, Where is the God of justice? (2:17). This is the answer, and it is better and more frightening than they expected.

First, a messenger who will prepare the way, like the men who went ahead of a king to clear the road. Some four centuries later a man in camel's hair appeared in the desert, and Mark opened his Gospel by quoting this verse of him (Mark 1:2), where it is joined to Isaiah 40:3 under Isaiah's name. Jesus said of John the Baptist, This is he of whom it is written, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face" (Matt 11:10). Malachi has before me; the Gospels have before your face. The LORD who promised to come is speaking to his Son: when Jesus came, God came.

Then the one the messenger precedes: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. It is his temple, and the coming one is the Lord himself. Haggai had promised that the glory of this second temple would surpass the first (Hag 2:9); here is how.

He is also the messenger of the covenant, the one who brings and embodies God's covenant. And there is a gentle irony in that phrase, in whom you delight: they say they want God to show up. They have no idea what they are asking.

Two questions, both expecting the answer "nobody", at least on our own record. Two homely pictures show what he does. A refiner's fire melts metal to burn off what is mixed into it. Fullers' soap was the harsh lye used by cloth-workers to scour grease out of new wool. Both are violent processes, and both are aimed at cleaning rather than destroying.

The small word sit matters. A silversmith sits beside the crucible and does not leave it, because metal left too long in the fire is ruined. God gives his full attention to the refining of his people, and he knows exactly how long is enough.

And look who gets refined first: the sons of Levi, the priests whose corruption filled chapters 1 and 2. God's cleansing starts with the people who handle holy things. (The ESV notes the end of verse 3 may be read "and they will belong to the LORD, bringers of an offering in righteousness".)

Here is the God of justice they had asked for. Sorcery and adultery and perjury, yes; and then, in the same breath, those who oppress the hired worker in his wages.

Underpaying an employee stands alongside sorcery and adultery, and so does wronging the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner. The root of it all is and do not fear me. Before that list none of us stands on our own record. The Lord who comes to his temple is the one who stood in our place, and the fire he brings is the refining of verse 3, so that those he has made his own are purified, not consumed.

God will be a swift witness. In a world where such cases never came to court, God says he has seen everything and will testify himself.

Who is “the Lord whom you seek”? The messenger is John the Baptist (Matt 11:10); the Lord who comes to his temple is Christ, the messenger of the covenant, who came to the temple as a child (Luke 2:22–32) and to cleanse it (John 2:14–16), and who will come again to judge (vv. 2–5).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition commonly identifies the messenger who prepares the way with Elijah, promised by name in 4:5, and understands the Lord who comes to his temple as God himself coming in judgment; some also link the messenger of the covenant with Elijah, for whom a chair is set at every circumcision. Both readings agree that a forerunner comes first and then the Lord himself. This commentary sees the forerunner in John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10) and the Lord's coming in Jesus, who came to his temple (Luke 2:22–32), so that when he came, God came.
verseByVerse.note: The messenger who prepares the way is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed (v. 6). Return to me, and I will return to you, and they ask, How shall we return? (v. 7). Will man rob God? — in tithes and contributions (vv. 8-9). Bring the full tithe into the storehouse ... and thereby put me to the test, to see whether God will not open heaven's windows (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's unchanging character is why his people survive, and he invites them to test his generosity by being generous.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed. From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts. But you say, 'How shall we return?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's unchangeableness is not an abstract doctrine here but the reason his people are still alive.

If God's love depended on his mood, or on their performance, this generation would have been finished long ago. Because he does not change, the promise made to Jacob still stands over Jacob's descendants, however disappointing they are.

James says the same of God: with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (Jas 1:17). And Hebrews applies it to the Son: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Heb 13:8).

Does God never change his mind, then? Scripture sometimes says God relented, as when Nineveh repented (Jonah 3:10). That describes his unchanging character meeting changed people: he always spares the repentant and always opposes the proud. His nature, purpose and promises do not change (Num 23:19).

Return to me, and I will return to you: the same invitation Zechariah had brought to their grandparents (Zech 1:3). God keeps saying it.

And the reply, How shall we return?, can be read two ways. It may be genuine bewilderment, or the defensive shrug of people who cannot think of anything they need to change. Given the tone of the book, the second is likely. God's answer is wonderfully specific: start with your wallet.

verseByVerse.quote: Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me. But you say, 'How have we robbed you?' In your tithes and contributions. You are cursed with a curse, for you are robbing me, the whole nation of you. Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need. I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your soil, and your vine in the field shall not fail to bear, says the LORD of hosts. Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who would try to rob God? The whole nation of you.

Under the law a tenth of the produce supported the priests and Levites, who had no land, along with the poor (Num 18:21; Deut 14:28–29). When the tithe stopped, the ministry starved and the poor went without. It was not a technicality; it was theft with victims.

Scripture ordinarily forbids putting God to the test (Deut 6:16), which makes this invitation to put me to the test a rare thing. The promise is agricultural: the windows of heaven opened means rain, and the devourer (the ESV notes this is probably a crop-destroying pest) rebuked means harvests that survive.

This passage is often misused. First, it is not a formula for personal wealth. God is addressing a farming nation under the covenant of Moses, promising national agricultural blessing for national obedience. To turn it into a guarantee that individual donors will receive money back is to promise something God has not promised here, and it has done real damage to real people.

Second, do not flinch from what the passage does teach. God notices what we do with money; stinginess toward God's work is robbery; and God is extravagantly generous, until there is no more need. The New Testament does not lower the standard but changes its spring: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7).

The test God offered Israel was not "give and get rich". It was "trust me with what is mine and see whether I let you down". Christians who give in faith find him just as faithful, though not always in money (Phil 4:19; 2 Cor 9:8). The spring of Christian giving is Christ himself: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). And for believers who are poor and can give little, Jesus counted the widow's two small coins as more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44); a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Cor 8:12).

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.
verseByVerse.note: The “devourer” is probably a crop-destroying pest (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have said, It is vain to serve God, and called the arrogant blessed (vv. 13-15). Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him (v. 16). They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, spared as a man spares his son who serves him (v. 17), and the distinction between the righteous and the wicked will be plain (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God listens to the conversations of those who fear him and writes them down.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your words have been hard against me, says the LORD. But you say, 'How have we spoken against you?' You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What is the profit of our keeping his charge or of walking as in mourning before the LORD of hosts? And now we call the arrogant blessed. Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last dispute, and it is the most honest thing they say in the whole book: It is vain to serve God. What is the profit?

They had kept the rules and walked around like mourners, and it had not paid. Meanwhile the arrogant were doing very nicely. It is the complaint of Psalm 73, and of every believer who has watched the unscrupulous prosper.

Note the assumption buried in the word profit. They served God as an investment, and they are unhappy with the returns. The relationship was commercial all along, which is why God's love in 1:2 meant nothing to them.

There is a searching question here for any Christian who feels God owes them a better life. What exactly did we think we were signing up for? The blessings of serving God are enormous, and most of them are not the ones on this list.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD and esteemed his name. "They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the grumbling, while the majority complained, a minority who feared the LORD spoke with one another. We are not told what they said. They were probably encouraging each other to keep going, reminding one another of God's promises, refusing the cynicism around them.

And heaven was listening: The LORD paid attention and heard them. Then this: a book of remembrance was written before him. Kings kept such records of loyal service. God keeps one too, and what he writes down is not great achievements but the conversations of ordinary believers who feared him and esteemed his name.

Two Christians encouraging each other after a discouraging church meeting, a phone call between friends about the goodness of God: that is what goes into the book.

They shall be mine. The word treasured possession goes back to Sinai, where God called Israel his own treasure out of all the peoples (Exod 19:5). Peter uses the same language of the church (1 Pet 2:9).

And the tenderness of the last line: I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. A father does not treat his working son as a hired hand. God's people are not staff; they are family. The New Testament shows what that sparing cost: God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32).

Their complaint was that there is no visible difference between serving God and not serving him. God does not deny that it looks that way now. He says the day is coming when the distinction will be unmistakable.

3.title: Behold, I Send My Messenger
3.overview:
To those asking where the God of justice is, God promises a messenger to prepare the way and the Lord himself coming suddenly to his temple, to refine his people like silver and to judge those who oppress the weak (vv. 1-5).

Because he does not change, they are not consumed. He calls them to return, exposes their robbery in tithes, and invites them to test his generosity (vv. 6-12).

Some say it is vain to serve God; but those who fear him speak together, he writes their names in a book of remembrance, and they will be his treasured possession (vv. 13-18).
3.theology:
God answers cynicism about his justice by announcing that he is coming himself (v. 1; 2:17).

God's coming is preceded by a messenger, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 1; Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10).

God's coming purifies rather than merely destroys, and he sits over the refining with full attention (vv. 2-3).

God's cleansing begins with those who handle holy things (v. 3).

Cheating a worker of his wages stands beside sorcery and adultery in God's list, and the root of all of it is not fearing him (v. 5).

God's unchanging character is the reason his people are not consumed (v. 6; Jas 1:17; Heb 13:8).

Withholding from God's work is robbery with victims, and God invites his people to prove his generosity — which is not a formula for personal wealth (vv. 8-12; 2 Cor 9:7).

Serving God as an investment leads to disappointment with the returns (vv. 13-15).

God listens to the conversations of those who fear him and writes them in a book of remembrance (v. 16).

God's people are his treasured possession and are spared as a father spares his son (v. 17; Exod 19:5; 1 Pet 2:9).
3.examples:
A road crew sent ahead of a king, four hundred years early.

A silversmith who sits by the crucible and does not walk away.

Harsh soap scouring the grease out of new wool.

Unpaid wages listed alongside sorcery and adultery.

A rare invitation from God: test me on this one.

People who served God as an investment and are unhappy with the returns.

Two believers encouraging each other, and heaven writing it down.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch.<sup>2</sup>But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall.<sup>3</sup>And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>4</sup>"Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.<sup>6</sup>And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Day Burning Like an Oven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: the day is coming, burning like an oven, when the arrogant and evildoers will be stubble with neither root nor branch (v. 1). But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings, and they will go out leaping like calves from the stall (v. 2), treading down the wicked (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The same day that burns the arrogant rises like sunshine on those who fear God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall. And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
(In Hebrew Bibles this chapter is 3:19–24, the end of chapter 3, so the verse numbers differ.) This is the day of 3:18, when the difference between righteous and wicked becomes unmistakable.

The picture is a clay oven heated white with burning straw. The arrogant — the very people the complainers had called blessed (3:15) — are the stubble that goes in. Neither root nor branch means nothing left to grow again.

The Bible is unembarrassed about this, and love does not require us to be embarrassed either. A world where cruelty and arrogance are never finally dealt with would not be a kinder world.

The book's last great promise: for you who fear my name, the same day is not a furnace but a sunrise. The dawn brings warmth and life, and this one brings righteousness, its rays spread across the sky like wings carrying healing.

Zechariah the priest, holding his newborn son John, prophesied that the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those in darkness (Luke 1:78). The sun rose in Bethlehem.

Anyone who has seen cattle let out after a winter indoors knows the next picture: awkward, delighted, kicking, running for no reason except that they can. That, not a solemn procession, is God's description of his people on that day.

The untouchable wicked become ashes, on the day when I act. God's people do not bring this about, and they are not told to. They wait.

Does this teach annihilation? The burning of stubble pictures the total, final ruin of the wicked. Some read it as their ceasing to exist; but Jesus speaks of eternal punishment (Matt 25:46), and Revelation of torment for ever (Rev 14:11). The better reading is that the image describes the completeness of judgment, not its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Remember Moses, and Elijah Is Coming
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember the law of my servant Moses (v. 4). Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (v. 5), And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The Old Testament closes by pointing back to Moses and forward to the forerunner of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel. "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With prophecy about to fall silent for some four centuries, God gives two final instructions. The first is to remember the law (the ESV notes the last phrase may read "and just decrees"), given at Horeb to a people he had already brought out of Egypt. Hold on to what you already have: that is God's regular provision for his people in quiet seasons: not new revelations but faithful attention to the word he has already given.

The second is a promise: Elijah, not necessarily the man himself but one in his mould, the prophet who confronted a whole nation's idolatry on Mount Carmel.

Some four centuries later, an angel told an old priest that his son would go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah ... to make ready for the Lord a people prepared (Luke 1:17). And Jesus said of John the Baptist, if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come (Matt 11:14), and later, Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him (Matt 17:12).

Some expect a further Elijah-like ministry before Christ's return (reading Matt 17:11 that way); all agree that the one whose way was prepared is Jesus Christ.

The book's last two names, Moses and Elijah, meet again on a mountain. When Jesus was transfigured, Moses and Elijah appeared talking with him, and the Father said, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him (Matt 17:3–5). The Law and the Prophets stood beside the one they had pointed to.

The book lands in the home. The last work described before the coming of the Lord is not a political revolution or a temple ceremony but the hearts of fathers turned to their children, and children's hearts turned back to their fathers. A nation is renewed one household at a time, and a revival that leaves families cold has not gone deep. And for those whose fathers failed them, God is Father of the fatherless (Ps 68:5).

The final words are heavy: lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction (the ESV notes this refers to what is devoted to the LORD for destruction). Our English Old Testament closes on the word "destruction", with a warning still hanging in the air and nothing yet done about it; the synagogue, finding the ending so stark, repeats verse 5 after verse 6 when the book is read.

Then four centuries of silence, until a man in camel's hair appeared in the wilderness: the messenger of 3:1 had arrived, and behind him came the Lord to his temple.

The curse hanging over the last verse of the Old Testament was not lifted by better behaviour. It fell on him: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The book that begins with I have loved you and ends with a threatened curse is answered by a cross, and the calves have been let out of the stall ever since.

Do these laws apply to Christians? Christians are not under the law of Moses as a covenant (Rom 6:14; Gal 3:24–25), but it remains Scripture, profitable for teaching (2 Tim 3:16). The Reformed tradition reads it in three strands. Its moral law, rooted in God’s character and creation and repeated in the New Testament, still binds (Rom 13:8–10). Its ceremonial law, sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, feasts, was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17; Heb 10:1). Its civil law governed Israel as a nation under God and ended with that theocracy, though its principles of justice still teach us.

Was John the Baptist Elijah? John denied being Elijah in person (John 1:21), which is what his questioners meant; Jesus said he was the Elijah Malachi promised, coming in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17; Matt 11:14). Both are true. It gives no support to reincarnation.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition expects Elijah himself, who was taken up and never died (2 Kings 2:11), to return before the Messiah; at Passover a cup is poured for him and the door opened, and the Mishnah (Eduyot 8:7) says he will come to make peace in the world. Both readings agree that Elijah's coming means the Messiah is near. This commentary follows Jesus, who said that John the Baptist was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), and so believes that the One he announced has already come and will come again.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament closes with a promise of Elijah’s return. Jesus said John the Baptist was “Elijah who is to come.” The “decree of utter destruction” means things devoted to the Lord for destruction (ESV note).

4.title: The Sun of Righteousness
4.overview:
The coming day will burn the arrogant like stubble, but for those who fear God's name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings (vv. 1-3).

The Old Testament closes by pointing back to the law of Moses and forward to Elijah, who will turn the hearts of fathers and children before the great day of the LORD (vv. 4-6).
4.theology:
The final day deals with arrogance and evil completely, and a world in which it never happened would not be kinder (v. 1).

The same day is a furnace to the arrogant and a sunrise to those who fear God's name (vv. 1-2).

Christ is the sun of righteousness who rises with healing, and his coming is the dawn Zechariah sang of (v. 2; Luke 1:78).

The proper picture of God's people in that day is calves let out of the stall (v. 2).

God's people do not bring the day about; they wait for it (v. 3).

In seasons when God seems silent, his provision is faithful attention to the word already given (v. 4).

God prepares the way for his coming by sending a messenger, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 5; Matt 11:14; 17:12; Luke 1:17).

The renewal God looks for reaches into the home, turning the hearts of parents and children to each other (v. 6).

The curse that hangs over the last verse of the Old Testament fell on Christ (v. 6; Gal 3:13).
4.examples:
An oven heated white with burning straw.

A sunrise with rays spread out like wings, carrying healing.

Cattle let out of the shed after a long winter.

A final instruction before four centuries of silence: remember what you already have.

A prophet in the mould of Elijah, arriving four hundred years late and exactly on time.

Revival that reaches as far as the kitchen table.

An Old Testament that ends on the word "destruction", and a cross that answers it.
